steps.title: D1 - T1 — Module boundary: a shared state object, not scattered module lets
steps.narration: app.js had ~15 top-level `var`s that every function could read AND write. Splitting into modules, I could have made each one its own exported `let` — but an ES module import binding is read-only in the importing module: `import { allEvidence } from './state.js'; allEvidence = x` throws, because only the module that declared a binding may reassign it. Almost every one of these values gets reassigned (not just read) from a DIFFERENT module than the one that first sets it — e.g. evidence.js does `state.allEvidence = data` after a fetch that actually happens in dataLoading.js. So instead of exported `let`s plus a setter function per variable, I put them all as properties on one exported `state` object: mutating a property of an imported object is fine, only rebinding the imported name itself is restricted. Same values, same semantics as the old globals — just relocated so the read/write rule is explicit instead of implicit.

steps.title: D1 - T2 — Loading the entry point as a module script
steps.narration: A classic `<script src="app.js">` executes eagerly, in the global scope, in non-strict mode, and has no import/export syntax available — every function and var in app.js became a `window` property, which is exactly why 6-7 of app.js's functions had to leak onto `window` again after the split, just to satisfy inline onclick/onchange HTML attributes that only ever run in global scope. `<script type="module">` instead: runs in strict mode automatically, gets its own module-level scope (so `js/main.js`'s top-level names don't become globals), is deferred by default (doesn't block parsing, runs after the DOM is parsed), and only this tag can use `import`/`export` at all — without it, every `import` statement in js/main.js and everything it pulls in would be a syntax error. It also only works over HTTP, not `file://` — same CORS-style same-origin restriction that already forced this app to be served via `python -m http.server` for `fetch()` to work.

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — classic <script> vs <script type="module">
steps.narration: Two behavioral differences that actually mattered here: (1) module scripts execute after the DOM is parsed, in document order, like `defer` — a classic `<script src="app.js">` at the end of body instead ran immediately, blocking parsing at that point. (2) A module's top-level declarations are scoped to that module, not attached to `window` — classic-script top-level `var`/function declarations do leak onto `window`. That's exactly why `js/main.js` has to explicitly do `window.navigateTo = navigateTo` and five more like it: the HTML's inline `onclick="navigateTo(...)"` attributes always execute in global scope, so functions the HTML calls by name have to be deliberately re-attached to `window` now that they're module-private by default.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — reading/writing allEvidence across modules
steps.narration: Before the refactor, `allEvidence` was a bare global `var` — any code in `app.js` read or wrote it by name directly. After the split, a different module has to `import { state } from "./state.js"` (see js/views/evidence.js:10) and go through `state.allEvidence` — property reads/writes on the imported object are fine (e.g. js/dataLoading.js:65's `state.allEvidence = data;`), but you can never rebind the imported `state` name itself, and a module that never imported it at all can't reference `allEvidence` bare. Forget the import and reference `allEvidence` directly in a module: `ReferenceError: allEvidence is not defined`. That error is actually useful — modules are strict mode and have no implicit-global fallback, so the failure is loud and immediate, pointing exactly at the missing import, rather than the old classic-script failure mode of silently creating a stray global or reading stale data with no error at all.
steps.before:
var allEvidence = [];  // app.js pre-refactor: a bare global var — read or
                        // reassigned directly, by name, from anywhere in the file.
steps.after:
export const state = {
  allEvidence: [],
  filteredEvidence: [],
  selectedEvidence: null,
  bookmarks: [],
  currentPage: "dashboard",

steps.title: D1 - Q3 (1/2) — named export: js/lookup.js
steps.narration: A named export (js/lookup.js: `findEvidenceById`, `findPersonById`, `findLocationById`, and four more not shown here) exports several specifically-named, equally-weighted bindings — there's no single 'main' thing lookup.js provides, so each helper gets its own named export, imported elsewhere as `import { findEvidenceById, ... } from "../lookup.js"`. Contrast with js/dataLoading.js:97's default export (next slide) — chose default there specifically because `loadAllData` really is the one and only public entry point of that module, whereas lookup.js has seven small, independent utilities and no such single 'main' export to prefer.

steps.title: D1 - Q3 (2/2) — default export: js/dataLoading.js
steps.narration: A default export is for a module with exactly one thing external code needs. js/dataLoading.js's `loadCorePeopleAndLocations`, `loadEvidenceData`, `loadTimelineData`, `showLoadingOverlay`, and `hideLoadingStep` all stay unexported — only `loadAllData` is ever called from outside the module (js/main.js:16: `import loadAllData from "./dataLoading.js"` — no braces, unlike a named import). Contrast with the previous slide's js/lookup.js, where seven independent, equally-weighted helpers each need their own named export instead.

steps.title: D1 - Q4 — why file:// breaks both modules and fetch()
steps.narration: Same underlying cause, two different enforcement points. Module scripts resolve each `import` as its own network-style request under CORS/same-origin rules — under `file://` there's no real origin to satisfy that, so the browser refuses to load the module graph at all (a console error like 'Cross origin requests are only supported for HTTP' before any of this code even runs). The app's own `fetch()` calls for `data/*.json` in dataLoading.js hit the identical restriction for the identical reason — no valid origin under `file://`. So: same root cause (no HTTP origin under `file://`), just tripped by two separate browser mechanisms — module resolution vs. runtime `fetch()`.

steps.title: D2 - T1 (1/2) — Reproducing the bug: baseline state before touching Evidence sort
steps.narration: Repro setup: I added a private note to E01 (“Morning calibration failure report”) and a private note to E02 (“Robot diagnostic log”) from the Evidence detail view, then opened Workspace. The Personal Notes list shows them in id order — E01 first, then E02 — and the hypothesis form's “Selected supporting evidence” picker below it lists all 18 items E01…E18 in that same original load order. Nothing here touches the Evidence catalogue's own sort control yet — this is just the honest baseline I compare against next.

steps.title: D2 - T1 (2/2) — Reproducing the bug: sorting the Evidence catalogue
steps.narration: From Workspace I navigate to Evidence and change only the “Sort evidence” dropdown to “Title (Z–A)” — I don't touch bookmarks, notes, or the hypothesis form at all. That fires handleSortChange() in views/evidence.js, which calls state.filteredEvidence.sort(...). Going straight back to Workspace afterward (no reload), the Personal Notes list now reads E02 then E01 — flipped — and the hypothesis evidence picker is now in full title-descending order (E18, E02, E09, E14…). A control on a completely different view silently reordered data two other views depend on. This reproduces every single time, from a fresh page load, with no timing sensitivity.

steps.title: D2 - T2 — Root cause: filteredEvidence aliased allEvidence instead of copying it
steps.narration: js/dataLoading.js's loadEvidenceData did `state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence;` — that's an assignment of the array reference, not a copy, so allEvidence and filteredEvidence were literally the same array object in memory. state.allEvidence is meant to be the canonical, stable list every other view relies on (Dashboard, Workspace's notes list, the hypothesis picker); state.filteredEvidence is meant to be a disposable, re-derived “current view” that the Evidence catalogue filters and sorts. Because they were the same object, handleSortChange()'s in-place `state.filteredEvidence.sort(...)` reordered allEvidence too. Normally getFilteredEvidence() (evidence.js) would break that alias the first time the Evidence list actually renders — it does `state.filteredEvidence = results` with a freshly built array. But a separate, pre-existing bug (state.evidenceViewLoading is initialized true in state.js and is never set back to false anywhere in the codebase — confirmed by grepping the whole repo) means renderEvidenceList() always takes its early-return branch and getFilteredEvidence() never runs, so in the current build that alias is never broken and the corruption is permanent, not just a narrow race. I confirmed this directly in the console (`(await import('/js/state.js')).state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence` → true before the fix) rather than just inferring it from the symptom. The fix: copy on load with `.slice()`, so filteredEvidence is independent from the very first assignment — exactly matching what getFilteredEvidence() already does on every real render, just applied at load time too. (The evidenceViewLoading stuck-flag bug itself is real but separate — noted for a later demo, not fixed here.)

steps.title: D2 - T3 — Verifying the fix: Workspace order now stays stable, nearby features untouched
steps.narration: I repeated the exact repro after the fix: seed the same two notes, note the Workspace baseline (E01, E02, full E01…E18 picker order), go sort the Evidence catalogue every which way (title asc/desc, date asc/desc), then come straight back to Workspace — the Personal Notes list and the hypothesis evidence picker never move now, confirmed via `state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence` reading false right after load. I also spot-checked the features nearest to this code: the Evidence detail panel (notes, status, relevance editing) still works exactly as before — opened via Timeline's quick-view “Open full evidence” button, since the catalogue's own card list has its own separate stuck-loading bug unrelated to this fix, left untouched for a later demo — and the Dashboard's evidence/people/location counts and the People view's per-person evidence counts, which don't depend on array order at all, were unaffected either way.

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — reference vs. copy, and how aliasing caused this bug
steps.narration: A *copy* is an independent array/object in memory holding the same current contents — changing one afterward doesn't touch the other. A *reference* is just another variable pointing at the SAME object — mutating through either name changes the one underlying object both point at, and `===` between them is true. Before the fix, `state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence;` assigned the reference, not the contents, so `state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence` was true (I re-confirmed live: false on the current fixed build, and it was true on the pre-fix commit bf8e25d). Because handleSortChange() in js/views/evidence.js calls `.sort()` directly on state.filteredEvidence, and Array.prototype.sort mutates its array in place and returns that same reference rather than a new array, sorting 'the catalogue's view' and sorting 'the canonical list' were literally the same operation on the same object — there was only one array to sort. The fix, `state.allEvidence.slice()`, makes a shallow copy: a new, independent array holding references to the same evidence item objects. That's the right depth of copy — I verified live that `state.allEvidence[0] === state.filteredEvidence[0]` is still true post-fix, which is correct and intentional: editing an item's status/relevance/note in the detail view is supposed to stay visible from both arrays. Only the arrays' element ORDER needed to become independent, not the item objects themselves.
steps.before:
state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence; // same array object — not a copy
// state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence  →  true

steps.title: D2 - Q2 — the exact trigger sequence, and could static reading have caught it
steps.narration:
Exact trigger, reproduced live: load the app fresh, add a note to E01 and to E02 via the Evidence detail panel, open Workspace — Notes list reads in the canonical load order (E01, E02). Go to Evidence and change ONLY the 'Sort evidence' dropdown to 'Title (Z–A)' — nothing else touched. That fires handleSortChange() (js/views/evidence.js), which runs state.filteredEvidence.sort(...) in place. At that exact moment, because state.filteredEvidence and state.allEvidence were still the same array object (the aliasing bug), the in-place sort reordered both simultaneously. Navigate back to Workspace without reloading — the Notes list and the hypothesis evidence picker are now in title-descending order, even though neither view's own code ever touched sorting.

Could reading top-to-bottom, without running it, have found this? Only partially, and it's not a fair 'obvious at a glance' bug. `state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence;`, read in isolation inside loadEvidenceData, looks like ordinary initialization — nothing on that single line signals danger unless you're already actively watching for reference-aliasing. The bug only becomes visible once you additionally know two more facts that live in a DIFFERENT file: that Array.prototype.sort() mutates in place rather than returning a new array (unlike, say, .map() or .filter()), and that handleSortChange() calls that mutating sort directly on state.filteredEvidence. Neither fact is visible from dataLoading.js alone — you'd have to trace every consumer of state.filteredEvidence across the codebase, recognize handleSortChange as one of them, and separately recall .sort()'s in-place semantics, to connect it back to the aliasing assignment three files away. That's a multi-file, semantics-dependent trace, not a pattern-match on one suspicious line — which is exactly why I found this by running the app and noticing the symptom (Workspace order changing after an Evidence-only action), not by reading the source first.
